references.text: Jacob kissed Rachel when he met her—kissing as a greeting and expression of love is an ancient custom that Jesus here refers to as something the host neglected.
Absalom took hold of people and kissed them—kissing as a greeting was a common cultural practice, which Jesus notes that Simon had not given him.
The king kissed Barzillai as a farewell—an example of kissing as an expression of honor and respect, what Jesus missed from Simon.
Paul urges believers to greet one another with a holy kiss—this shows that kissing was a common and important greeting among God's people.
The sinful woman who kissed Jesus' feet and anointed them—the direct context in which Jesus compares her actions to Simon's lack of hospitality.
Jesus begins his comparison with Simon by pointing out that he did not give water for Jesus' feet, while the woman washed them with her tears—a part of the same rebuke.
The next verse in Jesus' comparison: Simon did not anoint Jesus' head with oil, but the woman anointed his feet with perfume—further contrast between Simon's and the woman's actions.
Judas kissed Jesus to betray him—a sharp contrast to the woman's kiss, which was an expression of genuine love and gratitude.
Esau ran to meet Jacob, embraced him, and kissed him—a kiss as a sign of reconciliation and welcome, what Jesus expected as a basic custom of hospitality.
